title: Is prompt-based game generation just another abstraction layer?
author: Afzaalch00
selftext:
We’ve gone from raw coding to engines to visual scripting. Now tools like Tessala let you generate a playable game world just by describing it.

Is this the next logical abstraction layer in game dev, or does it oversimplify the craft?

At what point does AI generation become a legitimate part of professional workflows?

comments.author: OldTelephone320
comments.body: I see it more as a starting point than a finished product. If AI can handle scaffolding, that’s time saved. Creativity still comes from how you refine and build on top of it.

comments.author: moduspwnens9k
comments.body:
No. An abstraction layer is a set of rules that interface with a lower layer of rules. And being exactly a "set of rules" means it is deterministic.

AI is a new layer of *judgement* and this is novel

comments.author: Elegant_Gas_740
comments.body: I don’t think it replaces traditional development. It feels more like rapid prototyping on steroids. If I can generate a rough playable world in minutes, that actually frees me up to focus on mechanics and polish instead of boilerplate setup..

comments.author: MadwolfStudio
comments.body: Tessala is absolute garbage! Are you the owner? 😂

comments.author: Silly_Newt4788
comments.body: Full blown games from a single prompt is at-least 5yrs away - we have enough games as it is. We don’t need more games; what we actually need is how can AI help us be efficient.

comments.author: Dramatic-Quantity114
comments.body: Honestly it just feels like the next step. Engines didn’t kill coding, they just changed the workflow. AI will probably be the same good for speed and prototyping, but the real craft still matters.

comments.author: tschilpi
comments.body: Those tools can and will probably take over part of the production pipeline but what makes games fun is a fundamentally different problem. Fun in games is created through a tight core gameplay loops which builds suspense, anticipation, action and release. For this, a game designer has to curate the experience in a way that AI currently does not understand how to dp. So even if you can generate all the singular parts of a game world like its textures, physics, mechanics etc, it will still feel soulless and not be fun to play. Because fundamentally games are not about endless content or generation but about many other (less tangible) things and principles.

comments.author: darkluna_94
comments.body: It probably depends on how controllable these tools are. If something like Tessala can generate a starting point but still gives devs full control afterward, that’s powerful. If it’s locked-down automation, then yeah, it’s hype. The real value will be in how flexible these systems become.

comments.author: Business_Boss2942
comments.body:
It is already a part of workflow for indie creators but making it a part professional workflow is very difficult because they have been working on these workflows for very long and have created big communities around these flows so if they face any issues their are plenty of options to find solution but it is not easy to find solution to problems for new flows
Classic example is blender and maya , blender is free,easy to understand and highly efficient but still maya is the acceptable software in market because they have their pipeline build around it
